answer: Not effectively. In micro-batch, latency is the trigger interval plus the batch run time, so the trigger sets a latency floor. Each cycle also pays a fixed planning and offset-commit cost of about 1 second on a typical cluster. At a 100 ms trigger, almost all the time goes to that overhead, and below about 1 second the micro-batch model stops working. Sub-second latency needs a record-at-a-time engine, with a 10 to 100 ms floor, though it means a second runtime to operate. If the SLA is looser, such as several seconds or minutes, micro-batch with a suitable trigger is the better fit on the existing cluster.
